field: Copywriting (headlines, skim story, feature naming, voice, CTAs, honesty)

typefully-a.verdict: The headline names the exact unit of value and the small print has the driest, most specific writing on the panel. Fix one overpromise and it ships.
typefully-a.loved: "They read one line. Make it hookworthy." states the insight, then turns the brand name into the payoff. The receipt line "$10k stops the thumb. 3 years makes it believable." is the best single sentence across all five pages. The trust rows "Auto-DMs: Not a setting. Not ever." and "Auto-reposts: No surprise reruns." are dry and exact, and "Sharpening is free. Forever." is the most persuasive and most honest pricing heading in the set. "Sharpen my first line" is the most precise primary CTA: the product works on lines, not posts.
problems: The closing line overpromises: "Good ideas die in bad first lines. Yours won't." It guarantees an outcome on a page that elsewhere refuses to promise reach.

In the features section the biggest type is a list of module names ("Previews / Week / Inbox / Results / Review links"), which is SaaS filler. The real benefit lines are small, and "Replies come with answers." and "Your week, best times marked." read flatter than "already circled".
The 11 PM lede, "...and it goes out at 8:40 AM when your people scroll", sounds like autopilot. Say that you schedule it.
"Try it here" is a placeholder secondary CTA. Studio repeats itself: "6 clients, 6 voices, 1 inbox." sits right next to the H2 "Six clients. Six voices."
typefully-a.fix: Change the closing line "Yours won't." to "Yours don't have to. Sharpen one now, free." and change the secondary CTA "Try it here" to "See the receipts".

awwwards-b.verdict: The best skim on the panel: every heading is a two-beat line that moves the story forward. But the blue-pencil metaphor leaks into the nav and small print, where clarity should win.
awwwards-b.loved: Read in order, the headings make a complete pitch: "Write it rough. Post it sharp." → "Your facts stay. The fluff goes." (this answers the main objection early) → "Jot it at 11 PM. Post it at 8:40 AM." → "Start at $0. Stay for $12." → "Bring it rough. We'll sharpen it." The handwritten "that's fine" next to "rough" gives creators permission to write badly, and "The idea shows up late. Your people show up early. Hookworthy covers the gap." is the best lede in the set.
problems: It chooses clever over clear. Nav labels "THE EDIT / THE DESK", the carousel button "NEXT PROOF" and the line "Same paper, same pencil." are designer-speak. A skimmer can't tell what "The Desk" contains.

The story contradicts itself. The voice note says "the sizing thing. after a loss you size down. that's the post.", but the draft adds "so i think ... is honestly just". The drafter invents the filler that Sharpen then cuts.

The who-it's-for headings push each audience into caps eyebrows ("CRYPTO AND TRADING" above "Charts and P&L, minus the shill."). Skimming headings only, "Lead with the number." never says founders. Labels above headings are also banned by the brief.

The H1 never says "first line", so it could front any editing app. The brand promise "Good ideas die in bad first lines." is pushed down into the last lede. The all-caps mono CTAs ("SHARPEN MY FIRST POST") shout against a dry voice.
awwwards-b.fix: Use plain words in the nav and small print: "Sharpen / How it works / Features / Pricing", "Next example". Cut "Same paper, same pencil." Then make the 11 PM draft match the voice note instead of adding filler.

arc-a.verdict: The proven punchline on a page with no wasted heading. It's the safest copy to ship, just not the most surprising.
arc-a.loved: "Good ideas die in bad first lines." has stakes and specifics in seven words, and the closing "Don't let it die in the first line." calls back to it. Receipt copy like "The number and the three years do the work. Lowercase stays, it's how you write." respects the writer's voice. Feature headings like "Your best times, already circled." and "Every client sounds like themselves." are concrete, not filler.
problems: The hero receipt is muddled: "Made it a question. The reader answers in their head, then needs yours." Yours what? The section version, "The reader answers it before they finish.", is clearer.
"Start free. Pay when it works." reads as pay-on-results pricing, which it isn't. It's a soft implied promise.
Passive phrasing blurs who presses send: "Caught at 11 PM. Posted at 8:40 AM." Also "Replies come in with an answer drafted." is an accurate but clunky 7-word h3.
No heading names the receipt, the most ownable idea here. It's buried in the lede "names the move so you learn it too".
arc-a.fix: Change "Start free. Pay when it works." to "Sharpening is free. Forever.", and change the hero receipt's second sentence to "They answer it in their head, then read on to check."

arc-b.verdict: The best CTA and the most ownable idea (receipts), let down by a hero that says five things and one feature line that breaks the trust promise.
arc-b.loved: The secondary CTA "See the receipts" works two ways: internet slang for 'show me proof', and the product's actual receipt. "Every rewrite comes with a receipt." is the most ownable feature heading on any of the five pages. "X pays for posts. Not replies." is the only version that correctly names X as the payer.
problems: "Replies come in already answered." suggests auto-replies, which contradicts the "AUTO-REPLIES NEVER" row further down the same page. It's the worst line on the panel.

The hero says too much. The H1 and sub sit beside two handwritten asides ("That wavy line is Sharpen, flagging soft spots while you type." / "Every rewrite prints a receipt: the move, the why, what it cut.") and two stickers ("Free, unlimited", "Your facts stay"). That's five messages before the first scroll.
"Start free. Pay when it works." implies pay-on-results pricing.
The all-caps mono receipt ("STILL SOUNDS LIKE YOU YES") turns a dry voice into a shout, and "then wants yours" is vague.
arc-b.fix: Change "Replies come in already answered." to "Replies come in with your answer drafted." and cut the second hero aside so the H1, sub and demo carry the hero alone.

apple-b.verdict: Keynote fragments dropped into a creator's feed: tidy, forgettable, and the brand's best line is saved for the end.
apple-b.loved: The drifting feed of real-sounding soft openers ("hot take but i kind of think", "not to brag but i think i finally figured something out") shows the problem better than any headline. "It's not a strategy. It's a seatbelt." in the example thread is the best line on the page, and "Try a line" is a good, tiny CTA.
problems: "Write the line they stop for." is generic (it fits any copywriting tool) and leans toward a reach promise ("they stop"). The punchline "Good ideas die in bad first lines." is buried in the closing H2.

The headings are telegraphic ("Soft in. Sharp out." "One draft. Every feed." "Any niche. Same fix.") and need the visuals to mean anything. "Every feed" overclaims, since it supports four. "Any niche" contradicts "Traders first".
Feature labels are flat or misleading: "Idea caught", "Replies, answered", "Posted when they scroll". The passive voice suggests auto-reply and auto-post.

The examples are sloppy. "Nora Quill, ghostwriter for 3 clients" is paired with the trader's "$10k month trading" line. "Posts get paid. Replies don't." drops X as the payer. "Choose Pro / Choose Studio" is SaaS boilerplate.
apple-b.fix: Use "Good ideas die in bad first lines." as the H1 over the feed, and keep "Write the line they stop for." for the Sharpen section.

pickWhy: Its headline is built on the exact unit of value ("one line") and teaches the brand name as an adjective. Its receipts, trust rows and pricing heading are the most specific, dry, creator-to-creator copy on the panel. Its flaws are one-line fixes ("Yours won't.", "Try it here", "it goes out"), not structural.
combo: Keep typefully-a's page and headline, but take awwwards-b's skim headings ("Your facts stay. The fluff goes." for Sharpen, "Jot it at 11 PM. Post it at 8:40 AM.") and arc-a's feature headings ("Your best times, already circled."). Swap "Try it here" for arc-b's "See the receipts".
